html:
Surat, on the Tapi River in Gujarat, was the chief port of the Mughal Empire and for a time one of the busiest in the world. Akbar took it in 1573 after a siege, which gave the Mughals their window on the sea.

Through Surat passed the cotton cloth of Gujarat, indigo, and goods from all north India, sent to the Gulf, the Red Sea and Southeast Asia. Silver flowed back in. It was also the "gate of Mecca": pilgrim ships left from here each year, some owned by the emperor's family.

Europeans came for the same trade. The English East India Company beat a Portuguese squadron offshore in 1612 and was allowed a trading house, its first base in India. The Dutch and French followed. Indian merchants were far richer than any of them. Virji Vora lent money to the English, and the shipowner Abdul Ghafur ran a fleet as large as the Company's.

Shivaji raided the city in 1664 and 1670 and carried off huge sums. The English moved their headquarters to Bombay in 1687, the river silted up, and Mughal order failed. By 1800 Bombay had taken Surat's trade.

Today it is known for cutting most of the world's diamonds and for synthetic textiles.
